stem: Which statement best describes the Green Revolution of the mid-twentieth century?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The use of high-yield crop varieties, fertilizers and irrigation to raise food production in parts of Asia and Latin America, with environmental and social costs.
choices.explanation: The Green Revolution raised crop yields and helped feed growing populations, but it depended on costly inputs and had environmental consequences.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The development of nuclear power plants for farming, which supplied cheap electricity to farms across Europe, North America and Asia after the war and replaced the use of fertilizers.
choices.explanation: The Green Revolution was not about nuclear power.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A return to traditional farming methods without fertilizers or machinery, promoted by governments in Asia and Latin America.
choices.explanation: It involved modern inputs, not traditional methods alone.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A political movement to restore forests in Europe, led by environmental parties and farmers' unions in the 1960s.
choices.explanation: The term refers to agricultural technology, not a forest-protection movement.

explanation: The Green Revolution used improved seeds and inputs to increase yields.

stem:
> “With the internet and satellite links, a firm in one country can employ designers in a second, build its product in a third, and sell to customers in a fourth, all within a single working day.”
>
> *Source: Statement by a telecommunications executive, 1999*

The passage best illustrates which effect of technological change in the late twentieth century?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A return to local self-sufficiency in production, as firms relied only on suppliers and workers who lived nearby.
choices.explanation: The passage describes production spread across countries.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Communication and transport technologies reduced the importance of distance and enabled global organization of production and services.
choices.explanation: New technologies let firms coordinate across borders, supporting outsourcing and global supply chains.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The closing of national borders to trade, as governments restricted the activities of foreign firms and workers.
choices.explanation: The passage describes cross-border activity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A decline in the role of multinational firms, which lost ground to small local businesses in every country and ceased to operate abroad.
choices.explanation: The passage describes firms operating internationally.

explanation: The passage shows technology enabling global production networks.

stem:
> “All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. They are endowed with reason and conscience and should act toward one another in a spirit of brotherhood.”
>
> *Source: Article 1 of a declaration adopted by the United Nations General Assembly, 1948*

The declaration is best understood as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A statement of basic rights that later movements invoked, though the declaration itself is not a legally binding treaty.
choices.explanation: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights set out a common standard, and activists and later treaties drew on it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A document written by the League of Nations in 1919 to settle claims after the war.
choices.explanation: It was adopted by the United Nations in 1948.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A statement that rights depend on a person's nationality, religion and social class rather than on any shared humanity or common dignity.
choices.explanation: The passage states that all human beings are born free and equal.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A binding treaty that created an international police force to enforce human rights in every country.
choices.explanation: The declaration was not a binding treaty and did not create such a force.

explanation: The declaration set a standard of human rights, although it is not legally binding.

stem: Which statement best describes a development in women's rights in the twentieth century?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Many countries extended voting rights to women, and movements campaigned for greater legal, educational and economic equality.
choices.explanation: Women gained the vote in many countries during the first half of the century, and later movements pressed for equality in other areas.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All countries gave women full legal equality by 1900, so no further campaigns were needed.
choices.explanation: Full equality was not achieved by 1900, and it is still an ongoing goal in many places.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Women's rights movements disappeared after World War II, as their goals had been achieved everywhere and no group continued to campaign.
choices.explanation: Women's movements continued and grew in the later twentieth century.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No country allowed women to vote until the twenty-first century, when the first laws were passed.
choices.explanation: Women won the vote in many countries in the early twentieth century.

explanation: Suffrage and later campaigns for equality expanded women's rights.

stem: Which statement best compares the civil rights movement in the United States with the anti-apartheid struggle in South Africa?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The civil rights movement took place in South Africa and the anti-apartheid movement in the United States, and neither received any international attention, sanctions or foreign support from governments.
choices.explanation: The locations are the reverse.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neither movement used nonviolent methods, relying only on armed rebellion against the government and its army.
choices.explanation: Nonviolent protest was central to the American movement and used by many in the South African struggle.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both movements aimed to establish racial segregation in law and to expand the powers of the state.
choices.explanation: Both opposed segregation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both challenged legal racial discrimination through protests, boycotts and appeals to public opinion, and the anti-apartheid movement also relied on international sanctions.
choices.explanation: Both movements fought laws that enforced racial inequality, and external pressure played a notable role in South Africa.

explanation: Both opposed racial discrimination; the South African struggle also drew on international sanctions.

stem:
> “Wherever you travel, you find the same fast-food chains, the same Hollywood films and the same pop songs on the radio. Local traditions are being swept away by a single global culture.”
>
> *Source: A cultural critic, 1990s*

Which evidence would best challenge the critic's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Evidence that the same fast-food chains, clothing brands and coffee shops operate in many countries and in the largest cities of every continent, from Lagos to Tokyo.
choices.explanation: This supports the critic's claim.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Evidence that Hollywood films are shown in theaters and on streaming services around the world.
choices.explanation: This also supports the critic.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Evidence that local languages are disappearing in many places as children learn global languages instead.
choices.explanation: This supports the claim that local traditions are declining.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Evidence that people adapt global cultural products to local tastes, and that local music and film industries, such as Bollywood, have found global audiences.
choices.explanation: Cultural exchange runs in several directions, and local cultures often blend or reinterpret global influences.

explanation: Evidence of adaptation and of two-way cultural flows challenges the idea of one global culture.

stem: Which statement best explains why environmental problems such as climate change require international cooperation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only developing countries produce greenhouse gases, so only they need to change their policies and industries.
choices.explanation: Industrialized and developing countries both produce emissions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Climate change is unaffected by human activity and industrialization, so no cooperation is needed.
choices.explanation: Scientific evidence links industrial emissions to climate change.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Greenhouse gas emissions and other pollution cross borders and affect the whole planet, so no single country can solve the problem alone.
choices.explanation: Climate agreements such as the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement reflect the need for coordinated action.

choices.label: D
choices.text: International agreements can compel every nation to act, because they are enforced by a world government.
choices.explanation: No world government exists, and agreements depend on states' voluntary participation.

explanation: Pollution and climate change are transnational problems.

stem:
> “The chemicals used in refrigerators and aerosol sprays are destroying the layer of ozone above the poles. Unless their production is halted, ultraviolet radiation reaching the surface will increase and harm people and ecosystems.”
>
> *Source: A scientific report, 1980s*

Which international response is most directly connected to the concern described in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The establishment of the League of Nations after the First World War, which was meant to settle disputes and prevent future wars through collective security.
choices.explanation: The League of Nations was created after World War I.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Treaty of Versailles, which ended the First World War.
choices.explanation: The Treaty of Versailles ended World War I.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Montreal Protocol (1987), an agreement to phase out substances that deplete the ozone layer, often cited as a successful example of cooperation.
choices.explanation: States agreed to reduce and eliminate ozone-depleting chemicals, and the ozone layer has begun to recover.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Kyoto Protocol, which dealt mainly with the destruction of the rainforests in Brazil and Indonesia.
choices.explanation: The Kyoto Protocol (1997) dealt with greenhouse gas emissions.

explanation: The Montreal Protocol addressed ozone-depleting chemicals.

stem: The creation of the World Trade Organization (1995) and regional agreements such as NAFTA (1994) reflect which trend?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A return to mercantilist policies of high tariffs and strict state control of trade.
choices.explanation: These agreements reduced barriers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A movement to end all international trade and make every country self-sufficient.
choices.explanation: They promoted trade.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A plan to make all countries adopt the same currency and the same laws immediately.
choices.explanation: These agreements did not create a single currency.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Efforts to reduce trade barriers and promote the movement of goods, services and capital across borders.
choices.explanation: These institutions and agreements aimed to expand trade by lowering tariffs and setting rules.

explanation: The WTO and trade agreements promoted freer trade.

stem: Which statement best explains why many corporations moved manufacturing to developing countries in the late twentieth century?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Labor costs were much higher in developing countries, which attracted corporations seeking skilled workers.
choices.explanation: Lower labor costs were a primary reason.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lower labor costs and fewer regulations, with better transportation and communications, made it profitable to produce goods abroad.
choices.explanation: Companies could reduce costs and coordinate production across long distances.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Governments in developing countries banned all foreign trade, which forced firms to build factories there.
choices.explanation: Many developing countries welcomed foreign investment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The invention of the steam engine made overseas production possible for the first time in history, in the eighteenth century, in Britain and France.
choices.explanation: The shift followed late twentieth-century developments in transport and communication.

explanation: Cost advantages and better technology encouraged global production.

stem:
> “The free movement of capital has let corporations shift factories to wherever wages are lowest and protections weakest, while local farmers and workers are left to compete against giants. The gap between rich and poor grows wider each year.”
>
> *Source: A statement by critics of economic globalization, 1999*

Which criticism of economic globalization is best reflected in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It reduces all trade and isolates national economies from the rest of the world's markets and investors.
choices.explanation: The passage criticizes the free movement of capital, not isolation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It can increase inequality, weaken workers' protections and local industries, and give multinational corporations too much power.
choices.explanation: Critics argued that globalization benefits large corporations while harming workers and small producers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It eliminates the gap between rich and poor in every country that adopts it, which benefits all workers.
choices.explanation: The passage claims the gap is growing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It strengthens governments' control over corporations, giving workers higher wages and better protections.
choices.explanation: The passage argues that corporations gain power.

explanation: The passage reflects concerns about inequality and corporate power.

stem: Which statement best explains why diseases such as HIV/AIDS and COVID-19 spread rapidly across the world in the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased global travel, trade and urbanization allowed pathogens to spread quickly between regions.
choices.explanation: Faster and more frequent movement of people carried diseases across borders.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Medical research stopped in the twentieth century and no new vaccines or treatments were developed for any disease at all.
choices.explanation: Medical research advanced, although it did not prevent every pandemic.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Countries had become more isolated from one another, with fewer flights and shipments.
choices.explanation: Greater connectivity, not isolation, accelerated the spread.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Diseases spread only through wars between nations, carried by armies on the march.
choices.explanation: Disease spread through travel and trade as well as through conflict.

explanation: Global connectivity speeds the spread of diseases.

stem: Which statement best describes the Arab Spring that began in 2010-2011?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single election held in one country that changed the region and led to the spread of democracy to all its neighbors within a year.
choices.explanation: The Arab Spring was a series of protest movements across several countries.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A series of revolts led by the Soviet Union against Ottoman rule in the Middle East and North Africa during the 1950s.
choices.explanation: The Soviet Union and the Ottoman Empire were not involved in these events.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A wave of protests against authoritarian governments in the Middle East and North Africa, aided by social media, with varied outcomes in different countries.
choices.explanation: The protests began in Tunisia and spread to other countries, with some governments falling, others surviving and some countries suffering civil war.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A movement that produced democracy in every country where it occurred and ended all authoritarian rule across the Middle East and North Africa within five years.
choices.explanation: Outcomes varied widely, and many countries did not become democracies.

explanation: The Arab Spring was a wave of protests with varied results.

stem: Which statement best explains the growth of immigrant communities in Europe and North America after World War II?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All immigrants moved from Europe to Asia, where wages were higher and land was cheaper, so few people arrived in Europe or North America.
choices.explanation: Large movements went from Asia, Africa and Latin America to Europe and North America.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Immigration was caused by the collapse of the global economy in 1950, which forced millions of workers to leave their homelands and look for work abroad in other countries.
choices.explanation: Postwar economic growth increased the demand for workers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Migration from former colonies and developing countries, by people seeking economic opportunity or fleeing conflict, and demand for labor in industrialized countries.
choices.explanation: Both economic and political factors encouraged migration to wealthier countries.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Governments in Europe and North America forbade all immigration after World War II, so no immigrant communities could form in those regions.
choices.explanation: Many governments allowed or recruited immigrant workers.

explanation: Economic opportunity, labor demand and conflict drove postwar migration.

stem: Which statement best describes China's economic policies after 1978 under Deng Xiaoping?

choices.label: A
choices.text: China abandoned all trade and returned to complete self-sufficiency, closing its ports and factories to foreigners and foreign goods.
choices.explanation: China opened to foreign trade and investment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: China ended Communist Party rule and became a multiparty democracy with free elections, a free press and an independent judiciary.
choices.explanation: The Communist Party retained power.

choices.label: C
choices.text: China collectivized all agriculture and banned private enterprise, following the earlier Soviet model of central planning, state ownership and five-year plans.
choices.explanation: The reforms ended collectivization and permitted private enterprise.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The government introduced market-oriented reforms and opened the country to foreign investment while keeping Communist Party control, producing rapid growth.
choices.explanation: China combined economic liberalization with one-party rule.

explanation: The reforms opened the economy while the Communist Party kept power.
